name: Dermatitis
description: Dermatitis refers to inflammation of the skin resulting in erythema, itching, edema, and vesiculation, often followed by crusting and scaling. It includes a broad spectrum of disorders such as atopic dermatitis, contact dermatitis (irritant/allergic), seborrheic dermatitis, nummular dermatitis and dyshidrotic dermatitis. In Ayurveda, Vicharchika is one among the eighteen types of integumentary diseases, classified as a Ksudra Kustha (minor skin disease), characterized by mild to intense itching, papular eruptions, blackish/greyish discoloration and excessive discharge with predominant Kapha Dosha involvement.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Atopic dermatitis affects up to 20% of children and around 10% of adults globally, with increasing prevalence in industrialized nations. Contact dermatitis accounts for nearly 70% of occupational skin diseases worldwide. Seborrheic dermatitis is estimated to affect 1–5% of the general population but may exceed 85% in HIV-infected individuals. Nummular dermatitis represents approximately 0.2–0.5% of dermatology cases, while dyshidrotic dermatitis constitutes 5–20% of hand eczema cases globally. In India, similar prevalence patterns are observed, with a significant burden of atopic and contact dermatitis, particularly among industrial workers and urban populations. Morbidity includes chronic pruritus, secondary infections, sleep disturbances, and psychological impact, although mortality is exceedingly rare. Key risk factors include genetic predisposition, atopic background, impaired epidermal barrier, exposure to irritants or allergens, microbial dysbiosis, emotional stress, and environmental factors.

sections.title: Ayurvedic Correlation & Terminology
sections.content: Dermatitis/eczematous conditions can be considered under Vicharchika in Ayurveda. Vicharchika is a disease caused by the vitiation of tridosha with the predominance of Vata and Kapha. Acharya Sushruta mentions a Vicharchika type with Pitta dominance also, where there is minimal discharge, excessive itching and pain, and linear skin-lesions. As per Kustha Samprapti, the three doshas provoked by the particular nidanas creates shaithilya of Twak, Rakta, Mamsa and Lasika Dhatus. Further vitiation of doshas causes accumulation in the Shithila Dhatus resulting in Dosh Dushya Samoorchana. Based on the level of dosha-dushya involvement, various skin diseases such as Vicharchika are manifested. Dushivisha as well as Raktadushti may also play roles in manifestation of Kustha including Vicharchika.

sections.title: Clinical Presentation
sections.content: Table 1: Clinical features of different types of dermatitis — Atopic Dermatitis (chronic, relapsing pruritic eczematous lesions involving flexural areas with lichenification, xerosis; intense itching, red/scaly/oozing/crusting/cracked/thickened skin, sometimes bleeding on scratching; commonly affects children below five years; Dennie-Morgan folds under eyes; personal/family history of asthma, allergic rhinitis common; investigations: Serum IgE, absolute eosinophil count, skin swab, patch test if contact allergy suspected, skin biopsy in atypical cases). Irritant Contact Dermatitis (localized erythema, scaling, rough inflamed skin with burning/fissuring at site of repeated chemical/physical insult; often painful more than itchy, without spreading beyond contact area; investigations: clinical diagnosis, skin swab, patch test negative helps exclude allergic dermatitis, skin biopsy if diagnosis uncertain). Allergic Contact Dermatitis (erythema, vesicles, intense pruritus spreading beyond direct contact zone due to delayed type IV hypersensitivity; chronic cases show lichenification; investigations: Patch Test, skin swab, skin biopsy). Parthenium Dermatitis (widespread distressing dermatoses in rural and urban India caused by airborne allergen of Compositae weed Parthenium hysterophorus; mediated by type IV hypersensitivity with combined immediate type I and delayed type IV mechanism postulated; investigations: patch test with parthenium antigen, skin swab, serum Ig levels, skin biopsy if required). Seborrheic Dermatitis (erythematous plaques with greasy white/yellowish scales or crust on scalp, eyebrows, beard, retro-auricular area, sternum; may cause mild pruritus; exacerbates in cold weather, stress; common in Parkinsonism and HIV; investigations: usually clinical, KOH examination, skin swab, skin biopsy if atypical). Nummular Dermatitis (well-demarcated round/oval coin-shaped eczematous plaques, often exudative or crusted, primarily on legs and arms; intense pruritus; commonly in middle-aged to elderly men; winter aggravation; investigations: KOH examination, skin swab, patch test, skin biopsy). Stasis Dermatitis (develops in lower legs due to poor circulation from varicose veins leading to skin discolouration, thickening & leg swelling; reddish/brownish/grayish discolouration with itching, oozing, crusting or thickening; signs of chronic leg swelling; investigations: Venous Doppler ultrasound, skin swab if ulcer/infection, skin biopsy). Neurodermatitis/Lichen Simplex Chronicus (localized itchy skin condition with thickened, leathery, scaly skin caused by habitual itch-and-scratch cycle; investigations: clinical diagnosis, skin swab, patch test, skin biopsy). Dyshidrotic Dermatitis/Pompholyx (sudden onset of deep-seated tapioca-like vesicles on lateral aspects of fingers, palms, sometimes soles; associated with burning/itching; may fissure; often triggered by stress or hot weather, frequent recurrences; investigations: KOH mount to rule out fungal infection, skin swab, patch test, skin biopsy). Clinical presentation of Vicharchika includes Kandu/Atikandu (Itching), Pidika (Papular eruption), Shyava (Blackish/greyish discolouration), Bahusrava (Excessive/copious discharge), Lasikadhya (Excessive watery discharge), Atiruja (Excessive pain) and Raji (Manifestation of linear lesions).

sections.title: Clinical Examination
sections.content: A detailed patient's history should be taken focusing on: onset and distribution of lesions; inspection to identify skin rashes, redness, dryness, scaling, crusting, discolouration, thickening and other signs of irritation; severity of pruritus (e.g., keeping patient awake at night); family and/or personal history of the atopic triad (atopic dermatitis, allergic asthma, allergic rhinitis and other allergies like conjunctivitis); presence of contact allergens; presence of triggers including allergens (dust mites, animal dander), hot showers/sweating, soaps, fragrances, food hypersensitivities, and synthetic fabrics such as polyester. Classic physical examination findings of Atopic Dermatitis depend on age group: Infants develop oedematous papules and plaques that may have vesicles or crust on the scalp, face, and extensor extremities; infants rarely have lesions affecting the diaper area but may be susceptible to other causes of diaper dermatitis such as candida or seborrheic dermatitis. Atopic dermatitis children classically have fewer exudative patches and plaques on antecubital and popliteal fossae; adults have chronic lichenified lesions with predilection for hands. Individual lesions may be classified into acute (oedematous, erythematous papules and plaques and/or vesicles/crusting), subacute (erythema, scale, variable crusting), or chronic (thick plaques with lichenification and scale) stages. Clinical diagnosis as per Ayurveda: Darshana (Inspection) – Site of manifestation, Pidika, Shyava, Bahusrava etc; Sparshana (Palpation) – Rukshata, Kharata etc; Prashna (Interrogation) - Desha, Vaya, Kaal, Kandu, Ruja etc. Pariksha: 1. Dushya – Dhatu, Mala (Sapta Dushyas of Kustha - Tvaka, Rakta, Mamsa, Lasika, Tridosha); 2. Desha - Site of manifestation/ geographical habitat; 3. Bala – Pravara/Madhyam/ Avara; 4. Kala– Season/ condition of Skin (Navam/ Purana)/ Sanchaya, Prokopa, Prasara, Sthanasanshraya, Vyakta, Bheda Avastha; 5. Agni – Jatharagni (Mandagni/ Samagni/ Tikshagni/ Vishamagni and Pravara/ Madhyam/ Avara), Dhatavagni (Pravara/ Madhyam/ Avara); 6. Prakriti - Sharirika and Manasika Prakriti; 7. Vayas – Balya/ Madhyama/ Jirna; 8. Satva - Pravara/Madhyam/ Avara; 9. Satmya – Rasasatmya/ Okasatmya and Pravara/ Madhyam/ Avara; 10. Ahara – Digestive capacity. Other factors: Dosha Involvement – Vata, Pitta, Kapha; Involvement of Raktadushti, Dushivisha, Garavisha; Vata – Anuloma/ Pratiloma; Srotodushti; Misbehaviours/ Misdeeds done in the past may cause guilt feeling/ stress that can initiate or precipitate a Kusthasamprapti; Dhatus affected – from symptoms enumerated for each Dhatugata Kustha and Dhatu Dushti, the Dhatus affected are to be inferred and treatment planned.

sections.title: Differential Diagnosis
sections.content: Table 2: Differential Diagnosis of Dermatitis — Psoriasis (chronic plaques with sharply demarcated edge, acanthosis, parakeratosis, thick silvery scales typically on extensor elbows, knees, scalp; Auspitz sign positive, nail pitting, possible arthritis; investigation: skin biopsy showing Munro micro abscesses). Scabies (intense nocturnal pruritus with small erythematous papules, vesicles, burrows on finger webs, wrists, waist, genitalia; excoriations, secondary impetiginization; family members frequently affected; investigation: skin scraping with KOH/mineral oil showing mites, eggs, feces). Tinea corporis (annular erythematous plaques with raised scaly advancing margins and central clearing, possible vesicles at periphery; worse in humid weather; usually asymmetrical; history of pets or communal sports; investigation: KOH mount positive for septate branching hyphae). Drug eruptions (rapid onset of widespread symmetric erythematous macules/papules starting on trunk with recent drug exposure; may involve mucosa if severe; investigation: clinical history; skin biopsy shows superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate). Lichen planus (pruritic, purple, polygonal, planar papules with Wickham striae; commonly on flexor wrists, lumbar area, ankles; oral lesions appear as reticulate white patches; may have nail thinning or longitudinal ridging; investigation: biopsy reveals saw toothed hypergranulosis, basal cell vacuolisation, lymphocytic infiltrate at epidermal junction and civatte bodies). Insect Bite/Insect bite hypersensitivity/Bed bug infestations (common in children; localized reactions: itchy erythematous papules or wheals, central punctum may be present; may progress to vesicles or bullae; itchy erythematous papules often in lines or clusters; may have central punctum or clear fluid). Dermatophytid reaction (symmetric itchy papules or vesicles on hands or feet secondary to fungal infection elsewhere; often bilateral/symmetrical; lesions KOH negative, improve after primary fungal infection treated; investigation: KOH negative at eruption site, positive at primary infection site). Asteatotic eczema (very dry, cracked, fissured skin especially on lower legs in elderly during winter; fine scaling without well-defined plaques, minimal erythema, mild itching; investigation: clinical diagnosis based on morphology and seasonality). Pityriasis rosea (begins with single large herald patch on trunk followed by multiple smaller oval salmon-colored lesions along cleavage lines; mild itching, self-limiting; investigation: clinical diagnosis; biopsy rarely performed). Impetigo (honey-yellow crusted erosions often around mouth and nose in children, sometimes with bullae; spreads by scratching; investigation: bacterial culture positive for Staphylococcus aureus or Streptococcus pyogenes). Eczema herpeticum (clusters of uniform punched-out erosions on eczematous skin, often painful, associated with fever, lymphadenopathy; may progress rapidly; investigation: Tzanck smear showing multinucleated giant cells or HSV PCR positive). Table 3: Differential Diagnosis of Vicharchika — compares Vicharchika, Vipadika, Kitibha, Visarpa across features (Kandu/Atikandu, Pidika, Shyava, Bahusrava, Lasikadhya, Atiruja, Raji), chronicity, site of manifestation, dominance of Dosha, special characteristics.

sections.title: Investigations
sections.content: Table 4: Supportive Investigations — Essential: Detailed history and Physical examination; Complete haemogram (may show eosinophilia or other abnormalities of white blood cells, helpful to confirm atopic pattern; immunoglobulin profile may evaluate immunodeficiency or show raised IgE levels); C-Reactive Protein (increased blood concentration of inflammatory markers, strong marker of non-specific inflammation, influenced by age, BMI and smoking); Skin scraping with KOH (direct microscopic examination to detect fungal spores or hyphae); Skin swab test (to identify bacterial or viral infections that may superinfect the skin). Advanced: Patch Test (useful in finding cause of allergic but not irritant dermatitis; detects allergens responsible for type IV allergy; reaction graded 0 to 3+); Serum IgE Levels (total serum IgE and IgE antibodies specific to certain antigens measured using RAST; more than 80% of patients with AD have elevated IgE levels of >200 IU/ml; RAST may help identify specific dietary and environmental allergens); Skin Biopsy (important and not commonly performed diagnostic procedure to characterize nature of skin growth or eruption and assist histopathologic evaluation); Doppler Ultrasound (to differentiate dermatitis from other vascular or infectious conditions or evaluate cellulitis, venous insufficiency, or vasculitis; useful to assess venous insufficiency, reflux, or DVT which may underlie or worsen Stasis dermatitis). Table: Types of Dermatitis and Relevant Investigations — Atopic Dermatitis (Serum IgE levels, CBC for eosinophilia, Specific IgE if allergen suspected); Contact Dermatitis (Patch testing gold standard for allergic contact dermatitis, history of exposure); Seborrheic Dermatitis (usually clinical diagnosis, KOH mount to exclude tinea); Nummular Dermatitis (usually clinical, KOH mount to exclude tinea, patch testing if chronic/recurrent); Stasis Dermatitis (Venous Doppler ultrasound, CBC if secondary infection suspected); Neurodermatitis (usually clinical, skin biopsy if diagnosis uncertain); Dyshidrotic Dermatitis (KOH mount to rule out fungal infection, patch testing if recurrent or occupational exposure suspected).

sections.title: Diagnostic Criteria
sections.content: The diagnosis of dermatitis is primarily clinical and made after a complete medical history and physical examination. Dermatitis has varied diagnostic criteria in different types. Table 5: Diagnostic Criteria for each type of Dermatitis — Atopic Dermatitis: Diagnostic criteria proposed by the United Kingdom Working Party — consist of one mandatory and five major criteria, easy to use and do not require laboratory testing. Mandatory criterion (must be positive): An itchy skin lesion or parental report of scratching or rubbing of skin. Major criteria (at least three of the five should be positive): Onset below 2 years of age (not used if child less than 4 years old); History of skin crease involvement (including cheeks in children under 10 years); History of generally dry skin; Personal history of other atopic disease (or history of any atopic disease in a first-degree relative of children under 4 years); Visible flexural dermatitis (or dermatitis of cheeks, forehead, or outer limbs in children below 4 years). Irritant Contact Dermatitis: Diagnosis by exclusion — history of repeated irritant exposure, lesions confined to contact area, immediate burning more than itching, improves on avoidance; No positive patch test. Allergic Contact Dermatitis: Requires positive patch test (type IV hypersensitivity); Pruritic eczematous lesions often extending beyond contact site, delayed onset (24–72h after exposure). Seborrheic Dermatitis: Clinical diagnosis — chronic erythematous patches with greasy yellow scales on seborrheic areas (scalp, eyebrows, nasolabial folds, chest); Recurs with stress or winter. Nummular Dermatitis: Circular or oval pruritic eczematous plaques on extremities, frequently oozing; Diagnosis supported by negative KOH to rule out tinea. Dyshidrotic Dermatitis: Characteristic presentation of recurrent deep-seated vesicles on sides of fingers, palms, soles, intensely pruritic, often triggered by stress or seasonal factors.

sections.title: Evaluation & Assessment
sections.content: Various assessment tools used for the evaluation of dermatitis are presented. Table 6: Assessment tools for Dermatitis — Scoring Atopic Dermatitis (SCORAD): Assesses disease extent, severity of 6 clinical signs on a 4-point scale, and patient-reported pruritus and sleep loss, to a maximum score of 103. Atopic Dermatitis Severity Index (ADSI): The sum of 5 items rated on a 4-point scale (0-3): erythema, excoriation, exudation, lichenification, and pruritus. Six Sign Atopic Dermatitis (SASSAD): Six clinical signs are scored from 0 to 3 at each of 6 sites on the body. Dermatology Life Quality Index (DLQI): 10-item questionnaire assessing impact on daily activities and overall quality of life. Eczema area and severity index (EASI): Evaluates Area (percentage of body surface area affected by eczema) and Severity (intensity of eczema symptoms). Principles of Management: assessment of signs and symptoms before initiating treatment and the need for management through conventional treatment for associated comorbidities. If the patient is already under standard care, the physician may advise to continue the same along with add-on Ayurvedic treatment and can be assessed for the same in the follow ups for tapering or discontinue the treatment in consultation with the conventional physician. In Ayurveda, Kustha is an umbrella term for various skin diseases. It results from improper diet and lifestyle that significantly affect physiological and psychological well-being. The causative factors hint the involvement of Ama visha, Krimi, Rakta and Manas in addition to the Tridoshas. All the skin diseases are said to be Tridoshaja and is generally considered as chronic. The permutations and combinations of Nidana decide the Dhatus and Doshas involved, leading to specific skin diseases. Management may include Nidana Parivarjana (avoidance of disease-causing factors), Samprapti Vighatana (the process of disrupting the pathogenesis of a disease to facilitate its treatment and to facilitate non-recurrence) and relevant principles of Krimi, Visha, Visarpa and Jwara Chikitsa. The clinician should be able to diagnose the doshas and dooshyas involved and the level of involvement to decide the selection of drugs and duration of treatment. Samprapti Ghatkas: Doshas: Tridosha; Dushya: Twak, Rakta, Mamsa, Lasika(Ambu); Srotas: Rasa, Rakta, Mamsa & Udakavaha Srotas; Agni: Jatharagnimandya & Dhatwagnimandya; Srotodusti: Sanga & Vimargagamana; Sanchara: Tiryaga sira; Adhishtana: Twaka; Rogamarga: Bahya*; Swabhava: Chirakari. *Note: Kustha has a Sarva Dehagata nature. If treatment is delayed and is inadequate, it affects the deeper Dhatus. The Samprapti of Kustha is a complicated one. The aggravated Tridoshas move through the side-ward channels (Tiryakagata Sira) and are thrown towards the outwards from the Koshtha by Vata. So, the origin of the disease may be from Koshta, but it is considered primarily as a disease of the Bahya Rogamarga.

sections.title: Red Flag Signs
sections.content: These signs should be assessed before initiating treatment for need for management/consultation through modern medicine: Secondary bacterial or viral infection (pus, fever); Generalized erythroderma; Growth delay in children with Atopic Dermatitis; Severe psychological distress.

sections.title: Preventive Treatment
sections.content: (A) Preventive Treatment: The effective management of Dermatitis (Vicharchika) focuses on both preventive and curative measures, emphasizing diet, lifestyle and psychological well-being. Preventive measures involve Nidana Parivarjana, which refers to the avoidance of causative factors of the disease. Diet: It is recommended that one's Satmya Ahara (habitually suitable and agreeable food) be taken warm and fresh, avoiding preparations that are excessively dry or heavy. The food should be consumed mindfully, with proper chewing and at a steady, moderate pace. The intake of Viruddhahara (incompatible foods) may contribute to the onset of skin diseases; therefore, such foods should be avoided. Life style: Following Dinacharya (daily regimen) and Ritucharya (seasonal regimen) as prescribed in classical Ayurvedic texts helps in maintaining overall health and preventing diseases. Yoga: Dermatitis is a multifactorial condition influenced by immune dysregulation and psychosocial stress, where stress aggravates inflammation, elevates pro-inflammatory cytokines (e.g., IL-6, TNF-α), and delays skin healing. From a yogic standpoint, it reflects an imbalance at both physiological and psychological levels. Yoga offers a holistic, evidence-based approach by reducing stress and modulating neuroendocrine function through practices like Dhyana and Yoga Nidra, which help lower cortisol levels. Pranayama techniques such as Nadi Shodhana and Bhramari improve autonomic balance and reduce systemic inflammation. Additionally, Asanas like Tadasana, Trikonasana, Padahastasna, Ardachakrasana, Bhujangasana, Setu Bandhasana enhance circulation and support skin repair. Collectively, yoga exerts anti-inflammatory and immunomodulatory effects, while improving psychological well-being and quality of life. (Proper guidance from a yoga expert is essential before practicing yoga for skin disorders).

sections.title: Curative Treatment
sections.content: (B) Curative Treatment: Treatment can be initiated from the Poorvaroopa Stage itself. Preferably combinations/formulations containing Kusthahara property may be selected. Stages of treatment: • Elimination of Ama and kleda (process of digesting and eliminating toxins (Ama) from the body) by Pachana, Anulomana or Sramsana; Patolamooladi Kashaya and Phalatrikadi Kashaya etc may be used for Sramsana/Anulomana. and Chitrakadi gutika may be used for Pachana. • Agnideepana (concept of stimulating and strengthening the digestive fire ie, Agni) Examples: Agnitundi Vati, Ajamodadi churna, Shaddharana Churna etc. • Strotovishodhana (process of cleansing and purifying the body channels (Srotas) to remove blockages and promote proper circulation) such as Trivruta Churna. • Vyadhiviparita Chikitsa — Such as Manjisthadi Kashaya, Mahamanjisthadi Kashaya, Panchatikta Guggulu Ghrita, Khadirarishta, Sarivadyasava etc. • Rasayana (Rejuvenation and promoting longevity through specific treatments and lifestyle practices) — Such as Mahatiktha Ghrita, Madhusnuhi rasayanam, Bhallataka Rasayanam, Gandhaka rasayanam, Khadirarishta etc. • Krimi, Visha, Visarpa and Jwara Chikitsa as per the condition. Formulations such as Nirgundyadi Kashaya, Vidanga Churna, Vilwadi Gulika, Dushivishari agada, Dasanga lepa, Visha Taila etc can be used. • Nidana Parivarjana and Pathya Sevana — Pathya needs to be followed during and after the treatment. The line of treatment of Vicharchika has been classified into A. Shodhana chikitsa B. Shamana chikitsa. (A) Shodhana Chikitsa – Purificatory Therapy: Vata Pradhana – Sarpipan/ Ghritapana; Pitta Pradhana – Raktamokshana/ Virechan karma; Kapha Pradhana – Vamana. In Kustha chikitsa, purificatory procedures along with their frequency interval are described as below: 1. Nasya - every 3 days; 2. Vamana - every 15 days; 3. Virechana - every 1 month; 4. Raktamokshana - every 6 months. These may be performed as per the clinical condition of the patient and by assessing the feasibility.

sections.title: Shamana Treatment
sections.content: (B) Shamana Chikitsa - Curative Intervention: Shamana Chikitsa is intended to subside dermatitis in those patients who are unable to do Shodhana Chikitsa and/or are contraindicated for Shodhana karma. Shamana chikitsa is also done to subside the remnant Doshas after Shodhana Karma. External medicinal application/Bahi parimarjana: This can include application of Lepa, Parisheka, Avachurnana etc. External application of medicinal preparation in the form of paste/oil/ghee/decoction etc on skin lesion after performing Shodhana or Shamana therapies provides early relief.

sections.title: Management by Dermatitis Type
sections.content: Management of Atopic Dermatitis, Contact Dermatitis, Nummular Dermatitis and Dyshidrotic dermatitis through Ayurveda: Patients may present in the acute, sub-acute, or chronic stage of the disease. The duration of treatment for each stage may be individualized based on the clinical presentation and the extent of Dosha, Dhatu, and Agni Dushti. Atopic Dermatitis: Initial stage (14 to 30 days) — Ama pachana and Sramsana – Patolamooladi Kashaya; Along with Agnideepana, Prana Anulomana to be considered in the initial stage if associated with Respiratory symptom e.g. Sitopaladi churna, Amrutotharam Kashaya, water boiled with dried ginger/Jeera/ajwain for drinking purposes; Kledahara: Punarnavadi Kashaya, Gokshuradi guggulu, Punarnavasava (Especially in cases of weeping eczema); Dushivishari Agada can be given. Second Stage (1 to 2 months) — Agni deepana – Hinguvashtak churna, Agnitundi Vati; Rasa Rakta Dhatu Prasadana, Srotoshodhana – Avipattikara churna, Mahamanjishtadi Kashaya; Bahiparimarjanam – After Ama Pachana, Kashaya Dhara may be planned with Punarnavadi Kashaya, Guluchyadi Kashaya, Manjishtadi Kashaya etc for 15–30 minutes, followed by application of coconut oil; In cases of sleep disturbances due to itching, after the initial stage, procedures like Sirolepa and Takradhara may be planned, considering the season and the condition of the patient. Third Stage (2 to 3 months) — Manibhadra Gulam; Madhusnuhi Rasayana; Nalpamaradi taila, Eladi Kera – External Application. Nummular Dermatitis: Initial stage (14 to 30 days) — Ama pachana and Sramsana – Patolamooladi Kashaya, Phalatrikadi Kashaya, Avipattikara Choornam; Kledahara: Punarnavadi Kashaya, Gokshuradi guggulu, Punarnavasava, Punarnavadi guggulu; Agnideepana – Ajamodadi churna, Water boiled with dried ginger/jeera/ajamoda for drinking purposes. Second Stage (1 to 2 months) — Rasa Rakta dhatu prasadana, Srotoshodhana – Avipattikara churna, Mahamanjishtadi Kashaya, Patolakaturohinyadi Kashaya; Bahiparimarjanam – After Ama Pachana, Kashaya dhara may be planned with Guluchyadi Kashaya, Manjishtadi Kashaya, etc, for 15–30 minutes, followed by application of coconut oil; Sirolepa, Takradhara may be planned in this stage (7 to 14 days); Raktamokshanam - Prachana, Jalukavacharana. Third Stage (2 to 3 months) — Manibhadra Gulam; Madhusnuhi Rasayana; Mahatikthaka Ghrita; Gandhaka Rasayana; Nalpamaradi taila, Eladi Kera, Dineseladi Kera etc – External Application. Dyshidrotic Eczema: Initial Stage — Ama pachana and Sramsana/ Anulomana - Patolamooladi Kashaya, Avipattikar Churna, Drakshadi Kashaya. Second Stage — Thalapothichil/Takradhara – for 7 to 14 days; Vatapittahara medicines. Third Stage — Manibhadra Gudam, Mahatiktakam Ghrita, Khadirarishta. Contact Eczema: Allergic Contact Dermatitis — First Stage (7 to 14 Days): Nidana Parivarjana- Avoid Allergens/triggers; Application of Coconut Oil over the lesions; Internally, Patolamooladi Kashaya, Avipattikar Churnam, Dushivishari Gulika, Amapachana Vati. Second Stage (15 to 30 Days): Agni deepana – Chiktrakadi Vati, Agnitundi Vati, Amruttotara Kashaya, Amapachana Vati; Rasa Rakta dhatu prasadana, Srotoshodhana – Avipattikara churna, Mahamanjishtadi Kashaya; Bahiparimarjanam – After Ama Pachana, Kashaya dhara may be planned with Punarnavadi Kashaya, Guduchyadi Kashaya, Manjishtadi Kashaya etc for 15–30 minutes, followed by application of coconut oil; If the lesion is dry and inflammation is subsided then Nalpamaradi taila, eladi taila can be used. Third Stage (up to 1 month): Manibhadra Gulam; Madhusnuhi Rasayana; Indukanta Ghrita, Chyavanaprash; Nalpamaradi taila, Eladi Kera for External Application can be used. Irritant Contact Dermatitis — First Stage (0 to 7 Days): Nidana Parivarjana- Avoid the irritant; Cleaning the lesion and Application of Aloevera; Internal medications: Avipattikar Churnam, Dushivishari Gulika, Punarnavadi Kashaya, Haridrakhanda. Second Stage (Up to 14 Days): Internal – Guduchyadi Kashaya, Avipattikara churna; Bahiparimarjanam – Application of coconut oil, Nimba Taila if the lesion is dry.

sections.title: Treatment Levels
sections.content: Level 1: Solo Physician Clinic/Health & Health Clinic/PHC (Optimal Standard of treatment in situation where technology and resources are limited). Clinical Diagnosis: The diagnosis of Dermatitis (Vicharchika) is primarily clinical and made after complete medical history and physical examination, however, following investigations may be done to assess severity of inflammation or to exclude other diagnosis: Complete Hemogram; Skin scraping with KOH; Assessment of severity by different assessment tools such as SCORAD, ADSI, SASSAD, DLQI. Management: At level 1, treatment is solely based on Shamana protocol based on dosha predominance of clinical manifestation. Level 2: (CHC/Small hospitals (10-20 bedded hospitals with basic facilities such as routine investigation, X-ray). Clinical Diagnosis: Same as level 1. The case referred from Level 1, or a fresh case must be evaluated thoroughly for any complications. Investigations such as Serum IgE may be necessary to exclude other differential diagnoses or to investigate complications. Management: Based on the Dosha predominance, suitable medicines may be selected as given in Table 7. Purification/ other procedures (As per applicability): A general line of Shodhana treatment along with external therapeutic procedures is given below which can be modified according to the Dosha involvement and the conditions of the particular patient. Feasibility of doing the procedure at level 2 also needs to be considered. Shodhana: Deepana and pachana- with Shaddharanam churna or Hingwashtaka churna or Vaishwanara churna or Ajamojadi churna or Bhaskara lavana churna for a duration of 3 days or until the appetite is good; Snehapana- with Panchatiktaka ghrita or Aragwadha mahatiktaka ghrita or Tiktaka ghrita or Mahatiktaka ghrita - starting from 30 ml till Samyaka snigdha lakshana is observed (for a maximum period of 7 days); Abhyanga and Swedana- Eladi kera or Nalpamaradi taila or Nimbadi taila or any suitable oil as per Dosha involvement indicated for Kustha or Twak roga followed by Ushnambu snana for 1 day; Vamana- Vamana karma may be done with Madanapippali, Nimba, Vacha, Saindhava and Madhu (or) Vacha Yashtimadhu Madanapippali in Nimba swarasa with honey (or) Any other Vamana yoga specifically indicated for skin disease. Duration: One day; Samsarjana krama- Peyadi Krama should be suggested as per Avara, Madhyama or Pravara shuddhi for 3/5/7 days respectively; Virechana- with Nimbamritadi Eranda taila, Avipattikara churna, Trivruta leha, Triphala kwatha as appropriate taking doshavastha into consideration. Other internal medicines are stopped during Virechana and restarted during or after Samsarjana Krama; Samsarjana krama after Virechana as per Avara, Madhyama or Pravara shuddhi for 3/5/7 days; Sarvanga Kashaya dhara. Can be done with Aragwadhadi kashaya or Manjishtadi kashaya or Panchatiktaka kashaya or any other Twakdoshahara and Raktaprasadana kashaya; Takradhara - with Musta Amalaki takra or Aragwadhadi takra or Manjishtadi takra or Panchatiktaka takra for 7/14/21 days depending on the Dosha status. When Shirolepam is done, Amalaki and buttermilk prepared in Kashayasiddha Ksheera are used. Rasnadi choorna/Kachuradi churna with Dhanvantaram taila/ Bala taila / Nimbamritadi taila can be used for tailam; Marsha nasya- with Ksheerabala taila or Shadbindu taila. Takradhara, Shirolepa and Nasya help in alleviating anxiety and stress which is usually a comorbidity in all psoriatic patients; Prachhana/ Raktamokshana/ Siravedha: As per locations of lesions, Raktamoksha is done on Lalata, Hastapada or Shiras. Prachana is done in Alpadosha status. In Bahudosha, Siravedha is advised. In children Jalooka can be applied. All internal medicines are continued till Dosha and Roga Shamana. Upashaya Anupashaya may be considered. Rasayana drugs are started after Dosha and Roga Shamana and continued for a period of one to 6 months. Swastha vritta is to be followed during treatment and continued after complete Roga Shamana. Preferable Diet & Lifestyle: As mentioned in Table 8. Level 3: (Ayush hospitals attached with teaching Institutions, District Level/ Integrated/ State Ayush Hospitals). Clinical Diagnosis: Along with the newly diagnosed cases, the cases diagnosed at levels 1 and 2 that have multi-spectrum complications are addressed at the tertiary level. In level 3, the clinical diagnosis of Vicharchika is made according to Ayurveda, focusing on the Doshas involved in the pathology of the clinical manifestation. Although Ayurveda categorizes Vicharchika under the broad term “Kustha Roga,” it recognizes different varieties based on specific clinical presentations. Clinical Diagnosis will be the same as in level 1 and 2. Confirmation of diagnosis and assessment of severity can be done with the help of investigations such as Patch test (for allergic contact dermatitis), Detailed evaluation: Skin biopsy, Peripheral blood eosinophil count. Management: Internal and External Medications as per table no: 7. Purification/ other procedures (as per applicability): Shodhana treatment along with external therapeutic procedures according to the Dosha involvement and the conditions of the patient should be done at level 3. Subsequent Rasayana therapies should also be done after Shodhana therapy. In the case of Madhyama Dosha or Alpa Dosha Kustha, Samanoushadhi will be utilized as per Dosha dominance and Dhatu involvement. All internal medicines are continued till Dosha and Roga Shamana. Upashaya Anupashaya may also be taken into consideration. After Dosha /Roga Shamana, Rasayana oushadis should be started and continued for a period of one to 6 months. Preferable Diet & Lifestyle: As mentioned in table No: 8. Restricted Diet & Lifestyle: As mentioned in table No: 8. Follow Up: After every 15 days or earlier, as per need. Strict adherence to dietary restrictions (Pathya apathya) for a duration equal to or twice the total period of treatment should be advised. Naimittika rasayanas should also be administered during follow-up visits.

sections.title: Pathya-Apathya (Do's & Don'ts)
sections.content: Table 8: Pathya-Apathya (Do's & Don'ts) for Kustha (Skin Disorders). Pathya/Do's: 1. Laghu anna (Light food); 2. Tikta shaka (green leafy vegetables); 3. Ghrita (Ghee); 4. Mudga (Green gram); 5. Aadaki (Pigeon pea); 6. Yava (barley); 7. Godhooma (wheat); 8. Madhu (Honey); 9. Sali (Rice); 10. Karkati (Cucumber); 11. Triphala (mixture of three dried fruits, namely Haritaki, Bibhitaki and Amalaki); 12. Patola (Snake gourd); 13. Nimbapatra (Neem leaves); 14. Punarnava (spreading hogweed); 15. Khadira (Black catechu); 16. Tila Taila (gingelly oil). Apathya/Don'ts: 1. Dugdha (milk); 2. Dadhi (curd); 3. Kulatha (horse gram); 4. Masha (black gram); 5. Nishpava (green peas); 6. Ikshu (sugarcane); 7. Amla Rasa (sour fruits); 8. Virudha Ahara (incompatible food); 9. Adhyasana (overeating); 10. Ajeerna (indigestion); 11. Vishamasana (untimely food); 12. Vidahi (burning sensation), Vishtambhi and Abhishyandi ahara; 13. Matsya (fish); 14. Kakamachi (Black night shade); 15. Lasuna (garlic); 16. Tila (sesame); 17. Drava, snigdha, guru Ahara (liquid, unctuous and heavy to digest food). Vihara-Apathya: 1. Vegavaraodha (Suppression of natural urges); 2. Atapaseva (Over exposure to Sun); 3. Drinking cold water after direct exposure to the sun and after exertion; 4. Consuming food before the complete digestion of the previous meal; 5. Day sleep; 6. Stress; 7. Doing exercise or over exertion immediately after heavy meals; 8. Over exertion after Snehapana & Vamana; 9. Sudden change from cold to heat or heat to cold without following the rules of gradual change; 10. Sudden change from Santarpana to Apatarpana & Vice-versa; 11. Improper administration of Snehapana and Panchakarma Procedures. *These are general pathya-apathya guidelines to be followed in skin diseases. However, they may be tailored on a case-to-case basis, taking into account the patient's prakriti, type of Kustha, seasonal variations, and other relevant factors.

sections.title: Follow Up
sections.content: Clinical examination needs to be done during every visit - at least once in every 15 days or earlier as per need. Strict adherence to dietary restrictions (Pathya apathya) for a duration equal to or twice the total period of treatment should be advised. Naimittika rasayanas should also be administered during follow-up visits. Screening for complications or any other secondary infections evidenced by Atiruja, Atilasikasrava etc.

sections.title: Referral Criteria
sections.content: Level 1 Referral Criteria: Lack of clinical improvement after 4-6 weeks of individualized treatment; Extensive skin involvement (>30% BSA), especially in children or elderly; Severe pruritus leading to sleep disturbance or psychological distress; Severe pain with burning or stinging sensation; Secondary infection suspected due to oozing, crusting, fever, or lymphadenopathy; Diagnostic uncertainty (e.g., differential diagnosis from psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, scabies); Evidence of an increase in severity/complications; Coexisting systemic diseases (diabetes, hypothyroidism, renal impairment) affecting skin healing; Recurrent relapses despite compliance with therapy; Suspected allergic etiology needing patch testing or further evaluation; Substantial impact on their quality of life and activities of daily living. Level 2 Referral Criteria: Same as mentioned earlier at level 1, plus Non-response to treatment after 4–6 weeks of individualized therapy; Complicated or severe forms (e.g., eczema herpeticum, generalized erythroderma); Requirement for skin biopsy or histopathological confirmation; Presence of psychological disturbance (e.g., anxiety, depression due to disfigurement); Immunocompromised states (e.g., HIV, chemotherapy) complicating presentation; Referral if lesions are widespread, unresponsive, or infected; Autoimmune disorders with cutaneous overlap (e.g., SLE, celiac disease); Need for multi-disciplinary care (e.g., dermatology, allergology, psychiatry); Any other complication considered life-threatening by the investigator/clinician. Level 3 Referral Criteria: Same as mentioned earlier at level 2, plus Life-threatening complications, e.g., sepsis from superimposed infection; Treatment-refractory cases unresponsive to Ayurveda and supportive therapy; Severe psychological morbidity which needs inpatient psychiatric care; Integrated approach for cases with psychiatric distress or systemic complications; Uncontrolled immunosuppressive complications such as infections like Staphylococcus aureus, eczema herpeticum (HSV), and molluscum, ocular complications such as cataracts and keratoconus, telangiectasia, and acneiform eruptions, hypertension and nephrotoxicity etc; Suspicion of malignancy or precancerous skin changes (e.g., cutaneous T-cell lymphoma); Requirement of immunosuppressants or systemic antibiotics; Other modalities can be considered depending on the case.

sections.title: Clinical Algorithm
sections.content: Algorithm of Treatment Process for Dermatitis: Diagnosis through inspection and history → At level 1, Shamana treatment based on Dosha predominance → If Nonresponse to treatment / Development of Complications like secondary bacterial infection / Substantial impact on quality of life and activities of daily living / Diagnostic uncertainty → Yes: Start Shodhana treatment also based on Doshavastha, if applicable → No: Continue Shamana Treatment with Pathya apathya → If Improvement Yes: Continue regular monitoring and follow up treatment. If Improvement No: Sodhana and Samana therapy based on doshavastha along with the management of complications, if any. Regular monitoring & follow up. Consider Integrative Treatment → LEVEL 2 → LEVEL 3. General Line of Treatment: Elimination of Ama and kleda, Agnidipana, Strotovishodhana, Vyadhiviparita Chikitsa, Rasayana, Krimi, Visha, Visarpa and Jwara Chikitsa, Nidana Parivarjana and Pathya Sevana.

sections.title: General Instructions & Hygiene
sections.content: Keep skin dry and clean, especially in areas like skin folds, armpits, and groin areas. Hand Hygiene: Washing hands frequently with soap and water, especially after touching potentially contaminated surfaces or individuals. Don't share towels, clothing, razors, and personal care items. Foot Hygiene: Wear breathable shoes and moisture-wicking socks, especially in warm or humid weather. Dry feet thoroughly, particularly between the toes, after showering or swimming. Avoid Walking Barefoot in Public Areas. Clothing Choices: Opt for loose-fitting, breathable clothing made of natural fibers like cotton, which can help prevent moisture buildup. Allow shoes to dry out completely between uses to prevent fungal growth. Nail Hygiene: Keep nails short and clean, and avoid biting or scratching the skin, especially if you have an existing fungal infection. Hygiene in Communal Areas: Wash exercise clothes after each use.
